Review: Wild Dark Shore by Charlotte McConaghy (Audiobook)

by Joli November 18, 2026
written by Joli November 18, 2026
15
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:38
Instaread

I listened to Wild Dark Shore on audio and found it totally engrossing. Read on for my full review!

The Summary

A family on a remote island. A mysterious woman washed ashore. A rising storm on the horizon.

Dominic Salt and his three children are caretakers of Shearwater, a tiny island not far from Antarctica. Home to the world’s largest seed bank, Shearwater was once full of researchers. But with sea levels rising, the Salts are now its final inhabitants, packing up the seeds before they are transported to safer ground. Despite the wild beauty, isolation has taken its toll on the Salts. Raff, eighteen and suffering his first heartbreak, can only find relief at his punching bag; Fen, seventeen, has started spending her nights on the beach among the seals; nine-year-old Orly, obsessed with botany, fears the loss of his beloved natural world; and Dominic can’t stop turning back toward the past, and the loss that drove the family to Shearwater in the first place.

Then, during the worst storm the island has ever seen, a woman washes up on shore. As the Salts nurse the woman, Rowan, back to life, their suspicion gives way to affection, and they finally begin to feel like a family again. Rowan, long accustomed to protecting her heart, begins to fall for the Salts, too. But Rowan isn’t telling the whole truth about why she set out for Shearwater. And when she discovers the sabotaged radios and a freshly dug grave, she realizes Dominic is keeping his own dark secrets. As the storms on Shearwater gather force, can they trust each other enough to protect one another—and the precious seeds in their care? And can they finally put the tragedies of the past behind them to create something new, together?

A novel of heart-stopping twists, dizzying beauty, and ferocious love, Wild Dark Shore is about the impossible choices we make to protect the people we love, even as the world around us is ending.

My Review

Although I’ve owned Migrations and wanted to read it for years, Wild Dark Shore was my first read by author Charlotte McConaghy. I’m so glad I finally read something of hers because, man, it was one-of-a-kind.

The story begins with a mysterious woman washing up on the shore of a far-flung island near the Arctic Circle. She’s freezing and injured and needs immediate help from the island’s residents. Those residents are just a dad and his three kids, although you find out that there used to be many more on the island. In fact, it’s home to a research base and a seed bank where some of the world’s last remaining seeds for extinct or rare plants are kept.

Set in the future amidst a climate crisis, it becomes clear that this dad and his kids are under a lot of pressure to save the seeds.

There’s so much mystery going on in Wild Dark Shore. At the beginning, you really feel like there’s a lot of mystery and not a lot of answers. More questions than answers emerge in the first few chapters. Then, as you read, details are revealed in small bits. However, it’s also clear that some of those details aren’t the whole truth, deepening the mystery even further.

The questions just keep on coming. Why did all the researchers leave the island? Who is the woman (Rowan) really, and how did she end up on the island? What happened to the kids’ mom? What’s troubling the two older children so deeply? How did the radio communication to and from the island get wrecked?

All of those questions swirl around while the weather keeps warming and the seeds keep getting in more and more trouble.

Speaking of the weather, this is one of those books where the setting is one of the main characters. The descriptions of the sea, the storms, the wind, and the island paint such a vivid picture in your mind. The weather drives so much of this dystopian story and really adds to the ambiance in pretty much every chapter.

The audiobook had multiple narrators, adding to the whole experience of the story. I liked all of them and was really engaged and enthralled throughout the whole book.

I haven’t loved dystopian fiction in the past, but this book changed my outlook on it. When dystopian fiction is well-written and not ridiculously bleak, I can definitely get into it and enjoy it. Overall I give Wild Dark Shore 4.5 stars. I highly recommend it, whether you’re reading a physical copy or listening to the audiobook!
